title: Collection Combinators
story: Your boss hands you a massive list of numbers: 'Filter out the negatives, double what's left, and give me only the ones over 20.' You could write three separate loops... or you could build a pipeline of transforms. In functional programming, these are called combinators — and you can build them yourself!
why: Combinators — filter, map, collect — are the building blocks of data processing pipelines, and understanding how to implement them manually gives you deep insight into how collections transform data.
analogy: Collection combinators are like an assembly line: raw materials (Vec) go through a quality check (filter), then a transformation station (map), and come out as a finished product (collect). Each station does one job and passes the result forward.
try_it: Write a `filter_and_map` function that combines both operations in one pass (more efficient than two separate loops). Then chain three operations: filter positives, double them, and keep only values less than 50. Print the result at each stage to see the pipeline in action.
tips: Each combinator returns a NEW Vec — this is functional style: no mutation of the original data
Chaining creates intermediate Vecs — for huge data, consider combining operations into one pass
The pattern is always: create result Vec, loop input Vec, if condition passes, push to result
common_mistakes: Modifying the input Vec inside a filter/map function — these should be pure, producing new output
Nesting loops instead of chaining — filter_then_map is cleaner than a giant nested if-inside-while
Forgetting to handle the `None` case from `.get(i)` — even when you're sure the index is in range, match both arms
